flagged.evidence: The cited definition says only that the comparison functions are “polynomials p,q: N→N”; it does not require them to be nondecreasing. Step 1.2 infers m(x)≤p(q(|x|_tau)) from m(x)≤p(|x|_sigma) and |x|_sigma≤q(|x|_tau), which requires monotonicity of p. For a one-point instance set, take effective encodings with |sigma(x)|=0 and |tau(x)|=1, q(t)=t, m(x)=1, and p(t)=(t-1)^2. Clause 1 holds since 1≤p(0)=1, while the asserted conclusion gives 1≤p(q(1))=p(1)=0. Thus the written inference is invalid under the current definition.

This is the same unsupported monotonicity inference in the reverse direction. On a one-point instance set, take effective encodings with |sigma(x)|=1 and |tau(x)|=0, s(t)=t, m(x)=1, and r(t)=(t-1)^2. Clause 2 holds since 1≤r(0)=1, and the encodings are polynomially related (use the other comparison polynomial q(t)=1). But step 1.4 asserts 1≤r(s(1))=r(1)=0. No monotonicity condition for r appears in def-instance-size-under-an-encoding.

The concluding claim says L* is the least concatenation-closed language containing L and epsilon. Step 3.1 correctly shows that every concatenation-closed K containing L and epsilon contains L*, but the proof never establishes that L* itself is concatenation-closed: clauses 1 and 2 give epsilon∈L* and LL*⊆L*, not L*L*⊆L*. A short induction on the number of L-factors in the first word would supply the omitted qualification.
